entries.title: Stationarity of the patch optimizer
entries.claims: To build the small-patch subspaces, the paper minimizes the norm of an ordered product of regional filters. From the first-order conditions at the minimizer it derives that each regional output state is dominated by its optimal density plus a small shift, ρ_j ≤ x_j + b·1.
entries.found: QICLean proves the consequences of this inequality. The regulator is bounded by b·1 and by ρ, its trace by b·rank Q + tr((1−Q)ρ) for every projection Q, and hence by 1/4 at the paper's starting radius. QICLean #607 recovers commutation from shifted powers. The inequality itself, and the commutation of the minimizing densities with the outputs, are not yet derived for the ordered objective. Until they are, Proposition 4.1 is not formalized.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. This is the most delicate open step in Proposition 4.1, because the paper reaches the inequality through descending trace calculations on a noncommutative objective. The note warns against substituting a simpler separable objective.
entries.plan: Carry out the descending trace calculations for the ordered objective, derive the commutation and first-order conditions, and apply the regulator bounds already proved.

entries.title: Birth, death and exchange as allowed operations
entries.claims: Handing a region from one party to another (birth or death), or swapping ownership between two copies of the state (exchange), costs reference error at most L^−30 (4L^−30 for the exchange), provided the region shares information at most L^−60 with its surroundings. Each move involves only the named parties.
entries.found: Both lemmas are proved with exactly the paper's hypotheses, including the canonical maps, their contractivity and both error bounds. The moves were first proved as allowed operations only with the registers of each region grouped into one register. #8943 lists the registers of a frame one per site and per tag, each held by its owner, identifies them with the canonical coordinates, and proves the moves on that list: the birth is an allowed operation on the two named parties with one shared state, the death the same with one shared effect, and the exchange is the renaming, written as a reordering of registers that keeps every register with its party, followed by one private map. Each has the canonical map as its operator and the paper's reference error. No hypotheses were added.
entries.impact: None. Lemmas 6.5 and 6.6 are formalized as stated once #8943 reaches main.

entries.title: Rewriting a small patch as allowed operations
entries.claims: Lemma 6.3 rewrites the state near a small patch where ownership changes. It states that (1) the rewrite map is a contraction that moves the old reference state close to the new one, and (2) up to error L^−a the map is a polynomial sum of operations that the compression theorem allows.
entries.found: Part (1) is proved with exactly the paper's hypotheses. For part (2), Lean proves the branch expansion, the owner bookkeeping, the network of each branch with no wire from a vertex to itself, its truncation by Lemma 6.2 with error 2m/√k and at most k^(2m) terms independent of the site dimensions, and the final rescaling: for every δ > 0 there is a contraction within δ of the rewrite that is a sum of explicit product terms. Two steps are not yet formalized. Each product term is not yet written as an allowed monomial of Theorem 5.2. The registers of a frame, one per site and per tag, are now listed and identified with the canonical coordinates (#8943), with reorderings that bring any set of registers together; what remains is to read each product term as an allowed operation on them. The term count is not yet polynomial in L, because the patches do not carry the bound on the number of cylinder terms from Proposition 4.1.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. What remains is reading the product terms as allowed operations on the registers of a frame, and carrying the cylinder-term bound of Proposition 4.1 into the patch data.
entries.plan: On the registers of the frames (#8943), read each product term as an allowed party chain with the reorderings and the front-register calculus already used for Lemmas 6.5 and 6.6. Carry the bound on the number of cylinder terms from Proposition 4.1, with bounded numbers of patches and affected holes, to make the count of terms polynomial in L.

entries.title: Clearance during the dyadic repainting
entries.claims: When a dyadic square changes owner, each elementary move keeps a clearance proportional to the distance from a few marked points, with one universal constant a₀.
entries.found: Lean first proved the clearance with a₀ = 1/5000 for any guides with the properties the paper's proof uses. #8910 builds the schedule of guides, derives those properties from the disjointness of the bands, and proves Lemma 7.2 for every square of the hierarchy with no added hypothesis. Formal guides are labellings of the plane. On an interface curve they take the label on one fixed side, while the paper reads a boundary point after a small generic displacement into an incident chamber. #8935 proves the estimates for every guide read after one small displacement. #8970 identifies the paper's sampled guides with these readings. Every guide of the schedule is constant off a locally finite family of lines in finitely many directions, and a displacement parallel to none of them leaves them at once. So the sampled guides exist, are unique and equal the readings. #8970 states and proves Lemma 7.2 for the paper's sampled guides. It also proves the footprint ratios of the point treatment and of the block guides for them. The paper chooses ν before the scale D and the displacement after the guides, so its ν serves every generic displacement. #8974 proves the ratios in this order: two displacements on the same side of each of the finitely many wall directions give the same readings, so each template has finitely many readings after generic displacements, and one ν serves all of them.
entries.impact: None. Lemma 7.2 is formalized for the paper's chamber-sampled guides, with a₀ = 1/5000, and so are the footprint ratios for them, with one ν for every generic displacement.
entries.plan: Nothing remains for this note. The protocol of Proposition 7.1 is separate work.

entries.title: Who owns the replacement of a shared resource
entries.claims: Lemma 5.1 removes a two-party shared state by replacing it with a stack of m fresh copies, at error r/√m. It also states that the replacement uses only operations local to the two parties plus normalized shared states, and that all shared states between the same two parties can be merged into one.
entries.found: The first Lean model had no notion of a party, so the locality clauses could not be stated (#8791). #8843 added parties and proved those clauses. #8853 proves the merging clause. Each freshly prepared shared state can be moved to the front, and the states between the same two parties combine into one normalized state. No hypotheses were added.
entries.impact: None. Lemma 5.1 is formalized as stated.
entries.plan: Nothing remains for this note. The aggregate map per party used by Theorem 5.2 is separate work.

entries.title: Rectangles and triangles in a template are nondegenerate
entries.claims: Definition 9.3 builds a template as a finite union of the lattice points of closed rectangles and triangles of bounded size whose sides have slope 0, ∞, 1 or −1.
entries.found: Read literally, a segment or a single point could count as a degenerate rectangle or triangle. The paper plainly means ordinary rectangles and triangles: its remark after the definition says the estimates use the pieces only through their number and their sizes. Lean builds the ordinary reading into the definition of the permitted pieces, so no theorem carries a separate nondegeneracy hypothesis.
entries.impact: None. This is a reading of the paper's words, not an added hypothesis.

entries.title: The scanner estimate from the conclusions of its inputs
entries.claims: Proposition 9.2 says that, for one scan at scale n and every large replica count, some charge round and some interpolation parameter make the energy of the defect small, with explicit bounds on three comparator budgets. Its proof combines the scan geometry (Lemma 9.1), transport (Proposition 7.4), the comparators (Proposition 8.1), continuity (Lemma 2.1) and the spectral tails (Lemma 2.3).
entries.found: Lean proves the step from the conclusions of those five results to Proposition 9.2: the entropy balance over the charge rounds, the choice of a round and a parameter by averaging, the accounting of the defect energy at that point, and the three budgets. The five conclusions enter as one package of hypotheses, each transcribing one displayed statement of the paper. Two bookkeeping differences are harmless: one error term is carried as n^−247 rather than n^−248, and the unspecified logarithmic power is 12.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. The proposition holds for the paper's scan once its inputs are proved.
entries.plan: Build the package from the scan geometry of Lemma 9.1 and the transported states of Proposition 7.4, with Proposition 8.1 and Lemmas 2.1 and 2.3 supplying the rest. Each is a separate item of the campaign.

entries.title: Routing the party network with constant congestion
entries.claims: Lemma 8.2 states, with no hypotheses, that the links of the party network built by the distribution protocol can be routed on the grid with constant congestion, and that folding into the L × L square keeps the congestion constant and the physical outputs in place.
entries.found: The proof uses four properties of that network: every anchor lies on the padded grid, each dyadic block carries boundedly many parties, each party has boundedly many links, and linked anchors are close relative to their scale. The protocol of Proposition 7.1 is not yet formalized, so Lean proves the lemma for every party network with these four properties: congestion at most 8(2c+1)BΔ after folding, and the routed network is exactly a PEPS on the open square with bond dimension at most max(D,1)^(8(2c+1)BΔ).
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. The paper's lemma is the case of its own network, once that network is shown to have the four properties.
entries.plan: Formalize Proposition 7.1 and attach its parties to the anchors of the dyadic blocks. The first property follows from the attachment, the other three from items 1–3 of Proposition 7.1.

entries.title: Commutation of the transport metrics
entries.claims: Proposition 7.4 bounds how entropy and energy change as the replicas are transported across several bands. It assumes that the operators of different bands commute on the symmetric subspace of the replicas.
entries.found: The first Lean version required commutation on the whole tensor power, which is stronger. It can fail when two regions overlap without nesting: for three qubits, an explicit commutator is nonzero on the full tensor power and zero on the symmetric subspace. QICLean now restricts the operators to the symmetric subspace and assumes exactly the paper's condition.
entries.impact: None. The paper's hypothesis was the right one, and the first formal version was stricter than needed.
